facts.claim: First published in 1988 as The Psychology of Everyday Things; new preface 2002; revised and expanded edition 2013 (which added 'signifiers').
Doors: a flat plate signals 'push', a long vertical handle signals 'pull'. Norman borrowed 'affordance' from J. J. Gibson.

Norman argues that when people struggle with an object the fault is usually the design, not the person; a stove example: a wrong burner is caused by poor mapping between controls and burners, and redesigning the stove would prevent the error while teaching the user would not.
Chapter 5 is 'To Err Is Human' (slips, mistakes, designing for error). Norman argues for eliminating the term 'human error'.

Norman was called in after the 1979 Three Mile Island accident as a behavioural scientist to look at why operators erred. A secondary summary says displays were hidden from view and indicators misled operators into thinking cooling was working; operators were blamed for 'human error'.

Principles: visibility, conceptual model, mappings, feedback. Feedback means full and continuous information about the results of actions. The gulf of evaluation is the effort needed to read the system state and judge whether the goal was met.
Example in the book: recording on a VCR requires several steps beyond pressing 'Record'.
A conceptual model is usually highly simplified; it need not be complete or even accurate as long as it is useful.

Refrigerator: two controls, labelled for freezer and fresh food, suggest each sets its own compartment. In fact one sets the compressor level and the other shifts how cold air is split. A colder freezer also chills the fresh-food section; a colder fresh-food section takes cold from the freezer. Temperatures take about a day to settle. Norman says the controls suggest a false conceptual model.
Thermostat: people believe turning the dial to the top warms a cold room faster. The setting only decides when heating shuts off; heat output is the same.

Door anecdote in the first chapter: a friend of Norman's got trapped in the doorway of a post office in a European city. Secondary sources describe a row of glass swinging doors with an identical row behind them and no cues about which side to push. Colleagues coined 'Norman door' for any confusing door.
facts.source: excerpt quoted in Rosson and Carroll via search; 99percentinvisible; search summaries

facts.claim: Stove example: burners laid out two by two but controls in a line of four, so users pick the wrong burner; Norman blames the mapping, not the user. Light switches that do not match the layout of the lights are another example in the book.
The book began as The Psychology of Everyday Things; a blog says bookshops and libraries shelved it with psychology textbooks, so a later edition was retitled The Design of Everyday Things.

Three Mile Island nuclear plant, Pennsylvania, March 1979: the indicator for the pilot-operated relief valve was wired to the valve's solenoid, so it showed that a close command had been sent, not that the valve was shut; a downstream temperature indicator could have hinted at the stuck valve but operators had not been trained to look for it. Norman has said he was called in with other psychologists to help retrain the operators.

Seven stages of action: forming the goal, forming the intention, specifying the action, executing it (four of execution) and perceiving, interpreting and comparing the outcome with the goal (evaluation). The gulf of execution and the gulf of evaluation are the gaps between user and system.
facts.source: Wikipedia The Design of Everyday Things

facts.claim: The President's Commission on Three Mile Island found deficiencies in control-room design, procedures, training, management, operating-experience exchange and NRC regulation; the cause was never fully pinned on a single factor.
The gulf of execution is the gap between a user's goal and the actions the system requires; a reading lamp and its switch illustrate the stages of action in the book.
facts.source: Wikipedia The Design of Everyday Things

facts.claim: System image: all the information a device presents to the user; when it matches the user's mental model, people feel in control. A critic of the fridge example (essenceofsoftware) argues the real flaw is the controls themselves, since relabelling would not make regulation workable.
